title: Chapter 112 — The Blacksmith
paragraphs: Taking advantage of the mild, summer-cool weather now reigning in these latitudes, and in preparation for the particularly active pursuits shortly to be expected, Perth, the grimy, blistered old blacksmith, had not removed his portable forge to the hold again after the lengthening of the buckskin for the harpoon lines but still retained it on deck, fast lashed to the ringbolt near the forge, which was now fanned up to full blast.

A peculiar walk in this old man, a certain slight but painful yawing in his gait, had at an early period of the voyage excited the curiosity of the sailors. And to the persistence of their questions he had finally given in, and so it came round that everyone knew the shameful story of his wretched fate.

Belated and not innocently, one bitter winter midnight on the road running between two country towns, the blacksmith half-stupidly felt the deadly numbness stealing over him, and sought refuge in a leaning, dilapidated barn. The owner, finding him there the next morning, helped the frostbitten sufferer inside to the parlor, when long before he had been shivering on the road. And there the shivering man was rubbed and roughly revived, and his numb limbs soaked in warm spirits — a kindly restorative no doubt, but one that only too well thawed the frost from him, while the fire of the drink (since he had been a drinker) lit a worse fire in him than the one it had cured.

He was an old man who, at the age of nearly sixty, had belatedly encountered that thing in sorrow's vocabulary called ruin. He had been a craftsman of famed excellence, and with plenty to do; owned a house and garden; embraced a youthful, daughter-like, loving wife, and three merry, romping children. Every Sunday morning he went to a cheerful-looking church, planted in a grove. But one night, under cover of darkness and further concealed by his self-forgetfulness from the drink, the blacksmith's shop was broken into at one end and his home at another, and all, all was gone.

Oh, woe on woe! Oh, Death, why can you not sometimes be timely? Had you taken this old blacksmith to yourself before his full ruin came upon him, then the young widow would have had a grief delicious enough to slowly heal, and the merry children a care-free grave to visit. But Death plucked at a richer, a more bitter vine.

Why tell the whole? The blows of the basement hammer every day grew more and more between; and each blow every day grew fainter than the last; the wife sat frozen at the window with tearless eyes, staring blankly into the weeping faces of her children; the bellows fell; the forge choked up with cinders; the house was sold; the mother dived down into the long church-yard grass; her children twice followed her there; and the houseless, familyless old man staggered off a vagabond in crape; his every woe unremedied. Death seems the only fitting sequel for a career like this.

Death seems the only desirable sequel for a career like this; but Death is only a launching into the region of the strange Untried; it is but the first greeting to the possibilities of the immense Remote, the Wild, the Watery, the Unshored. Therefore, to the death-longing eyes of such men who still have left in them some interior compulsion to live, the all-contributing and all-accommodating ocean beckons with wide-open arms. Because there, in a limitless, indefinite manner as in no other place, those things that are equally dangerous and dispiriting in the land feel oddly different from the sea; they smell less acutely there, and there lose half their terror. It is this that drives men to sea.
Hearkening to these voices, East and West, by early sunrise and by fall of evening, the blacksmith's soul responded: Aye, I come! And so Perth went a-whaling.
